name: Iron Man Armor
summary: Tony Stark's powered suit began as a clunky grey shell built in captivity and became a long line of armours: space suits, Hulkbusters, and finally nanotech that lives inside his body.

parts.label: Helmet & HUD
parts.fact: On film, the faceplate hides a heads-up display run by Stark's AI butler J.A.R.V.I.S., voiced by Paul Bettany, who talks Tony through flights and fights.

parts.label: Chest reactor
parts.fact: On film, Iron Man 2 (2010) reveals that the palladium core of his chest arc reactor is slowly poisoning Tony, until he synthesises a brand-new element to replace it.

parts.label: Gauntlets
parts.fact: In the comics, the Bleeding Edge armour (2010) puts repulsors in the palms, knuckles, chest, back and legs, and the emitters double as cameras for an all-round view.

parts.label: Legs & boot jets
parts.fact: On film, the silver Mark II took a reckless high-altitude test flight and iced up, nearly crashing; the fix was a gold-titanium alloy used on the next suit.

parts.label: Back & flight
parts.fact: In the comics, the Space Armor of Iron Man #142 (1981) was the first suit purpose-built for flying and fighting beyond Earth's atmosphere.

parts.label: Under-suit
parts.fact: In the comics, Extremis (2005) wove part of the armour into Tony's own body; Bleeding Edge (2010) goes further, storing the whole suit inside him as nanoparticles.

trivia: Jack Kirby designed the bulky grey original; it was painted gold in the very next issue, Tales of Suspense #40.
Steve Ditko's sleeker redesign in Tales of Suspense #48 (1963) introduced the red-and-gold look that stuck.
The red-and-silver Silver Centurion armour arrived in the landmark Iron Man #200 (1985).
The dedicated Hulkbuster armour got its comics showcase in World War Hulk #1 (2007), built for exactly one job.
On film, the Mark III's alloy was borrowed from a Stark Industries military satellite called Seraphim.
